title: Dilavar Khan Claims the Plateau
subtitle: When Delhi Fell Silent, Mandu Found Its Voice
era: Breakaway from Delhi after Timur, c. 1390s-1405 CE
region: Dhar, Mandu and the Malwa plateau
moral: A new state often begins when a frontier learns to stand alone.

sources.citation: Dilavar Khan Mosque inscription at Mandu, AH 808 / 1405-06, published in Epigraphia Indo-Moslemica
sources.note: Contemporary epigraphic anchor for the earliest Mandu building phase.

sources.citation: Yahya ibn Ahmad Sirhindi, Tarikh-i-Mubarak Shahi, c. 1434
sources.note: Near-contemporary Delhi-centered witness to the loosening of Tughluq authority.

sources.citation: Subhash Parihar, Some Aspects of Indo-Islamic Architecture (1999); Simon Digby on post-Tughluq successor states
sources.note: Modern framing of Mandu as a successor-state capital, not an empty new site.

panels.shot: sweeping low-angle wide of Mandu’s cliff edge at dusk

dialogue.text: In the years after Timur’s sack of Delhi, as the old capital lay broken, Dilavar Khan Ghuri turned his face to Mandu and quietly made Malwa a kingdom in all but name.

panels.shot: wide aerial over Delhi’s ruined quarters, smoky, desolate

dialogue.text: In 1398, Timur’s army fell upon Delhi. Chronicles remember streets emptied, quarters burned, and a Sultanate shaken to its core.

panels.shot: medium shot inside a dim audience hall in Delhi

dialogue.text: Before the storm, Dilavar Khan had ruled Malwa for Delhi. He was no newcomer from distant Ghur now, but the head of a local military lineage rooted in the plateau.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Dilavar Khan’s contemplative face

dialogue.text: Yahya Sirhindi would later note how, as Delhi’s hold loosened, provincial governors began to act on their own. Malwa was already watching this shift.

panels.shot: wide shot of a road leaving Delhi towards the south

dialogue.text: From the ruined capital he returned to his charge. Between Delhi’s orders and Malwa’s survival, a choice was beginning to form.

panels.shot: panoramic wide of the Malwa plateau and city of Dhar

dialogue.text: For years, Dhar had been Malwa’s seat. Forts, shrines, and markets lay across its gentle rises, while the harsher cliffs of Mandu watched from the horizon.

panels.shot: high-angle shot over the edge of Mandu’s cliffs

dialogue.text: Mandu—Mandavgarh—was no empty rock. Paramara builders had raised walls and temples here. The plateau held older meanings and proven strength.

panels.shot: medium shot among stones of old fortifications

dialogue.text: Subhash Parihar and other scholars note how Sultanate builders reused this landscape. Mandu’s rise was a layering, not a replacement, of past with present.

panels.shot: interior wide shot of a council in a fortified room in Mandu

dialogue.speaker: dilavar_khan_ghuri
dialogue.text: Delhi calls, but its voice is faint. Malwa must stand on its own feet.

panels.shot: wide shot of construction activity on Mandu plateau

dialogue.text: Between about 1401 and 1405, power shifted. Dhar faded as Mandu’s fortifications thickened, its halls expanded, its water systems renewed for a long siege if needed.

panels.shot: medium shot of artisans at work on mosque arches

dialogue.text: In AH 808—1405–06—the inscription of the Dilavar Khan Mosque was set in stone. It fixed his name in Mandu’s fabric, a governor now building as a sovereign.

panels.shot: close-up on Dilavar Khan Mosque inscription

dialogue.text: Epigraphia Indo-Moslemica preserves the verse that names him. A quiet line, but it marks Mandu’s first clear architectural claim as a capital.

panels.shot: wide shot of Friday congregation in the mosque courtyard

dialogue.text: From Delhi, no strong hand now reached to correct him. His khutba and coin followed local needs, and Yahya’s chronicle reflects this loosening from the center.

panels.shot: medium shot of Dilavar Khan addressing officers after prayer

dialogue.speaker: dilavar_khan_ghuri
dialogue.text: Our duty is here—Malwa’s fields, Malwa’s towns. We will guard them as our own.

panels.shot: bird’s-eye view of Malwa plateau showing Mandu’s dominance

dialogue.text: Simon Digby and others see Mandu now among Delhi’s successor states: not a rebel camp, but a regional center that had learned to rule in the old capital’s silence.

panels.shot: medium shot of Dilavar Khan in an audience hall in Mandu

dialogue.text: He did not yet style himself with grand imperial titles. But in tax, justice, and defense, Malwa’s decisions now began and ended in Mandu.

panels.shot: low-angle shot of Dilavar Khan standing by a window overlooking the plateau

dialogue.text: Between the records there is no single date when Malwa ‘became’ a kingdom. Instead, step by step, its frontier learned to stand alone.

panels.shot: transition shot dissolving from Dilavar Khan to later Mandu palaces

dialogue.text: Dilavar Khan would be followed by rulers with greater splendor. Yet the decision to choose Mandu as Malwa’s heart was his, carved first in cautious stone.

panels.shot: final wide shot of Mandu at sunset, timeless and still

dialogue.text: Today, standing on Mandu’s edge, we see more than ruins; we see the moment when a broken empire’s frontier found the courage to become a state.
